meaning: N. of a Buddha of an author, an immense number, said by Buddhists to be 100 vivaras.

pronunciation.approximation: uk-SHOH-bhyuh — the kṣ is a single conjunct sound (k + retroflex ṣ); the bh is aspirated.
pronunciation.note: Akṣobhya is a-privative plus kṣobhya, "to be shaken" — from √kṣubh, "to shake, agitate" (Monier-Williams): "the Unshakable, the Immovable." The name states his defining vow: never to give way to anger. The restoration keeps the kṣ conjunct with its retroflex ṣ exactly as the Sanskrit writes it; the ASCII "Akshobhya" transliterates the letter but loses its shape. Tier-1 by rule: the retroflex ṣ is a distinctive letter.

domains.title: The Unshakable
domains.subtitle: The Eastern Pure Land, the Mirror-Like Wisdom, and the Vow Against Anger
domains.lead: Akṣobhya is the Buddha who cannot be shaken: lord of Abhirati, the eastern Land of Delight, blue as the vajra family he heads, seated in the earth-touching gesture — the one of the five tathāgatas who turns the poison of hatred into the mirror-like wisdom that reflects everything and is disturbed by nothing.

cards.name: Abhirati
cards.desc: The Land of Delight in the east — his Buddha-field, open to all who aspire to be reborn there.

cards.name: The Mirror-Like Wisdom
cards.desc: Ādarśa-jñāna: awareness that shows all things exactly as they are, and holds none of them.

cards.name: Bhūmisparśa
cards.desc: The earth-touching mudrā — the awakening gesture itself, his seal among the five.

cards.name: The Vajra Family
cards.desc: Head of the vajra clan of the five tathāgatas: blue, eastern, indestructible as the thunderbolt.

symbols.name: The blue vajra
symbols.meaning: Indestructibility: the thunderbolt that is also the diamond, his family and his nature

mythology.lead: Akṣobhya's mythology is the story of a single vow kept without a crack: the monk who resolved never to be angry, and became the Buddha of the unshakable land.

myths.title: The Vow Against Anger
myths.text: His sūtra — the Akṣobhya-tathāgatasya-vyūha, among the earliest pure-land scriptures translated into Chinese, carried over by Lokakṣema in the second century CE — tells how a monk of a past age stood before a Buddha and vowed that until his own awakening he would never give rise to anger or malice toward any being. From that vow came his name: Akṣobhya, the Unshakable. The text then shows the vow fulfilled: the monk is now the Buddha of Abhirati, and beings who aspire to his land are promised rebirth where anger finds no purchase.

myths.title: The Land of Delight
myths.text: Abhirati, "the Delightful," is the east's answer to Sukhāvatī: a Buddha-field without the evil rebirths, level and fragrant, beautiful beyond the worlds men know. The sūtra lavishes detail on its gentleness — no lower destinies, no sickness as we know it, and women, the text takes care to say, bear children there without pain. It is the pure land of moral steadiness: not escape from the world, but a world where steadiness is finally possible.

myths.title: The Mirror of the East
myths.text: In the mandala of the five tathāgatas — Vairocana at the center, Akṣobhya east, Ratnasambhava south, Amitābha west, Amoghasiddhi north — each Buddha governs a poison and transmutes it. Akṣobhya's poison is hatred (dveṣa), and his transmutation is the ādarśa-jñāna, the mirror-like wisdom: the mind that reflects anger, insult, and loss exactly as they are, like a mirror showing a storm, and is not stormed. Blue, vajra-clan, elephant-borne, earth-touching: the whole iconography says one thing — unmoved.

myths.title: Lord of the Vajra Clan
myths.text: In the Highest Yoga Tantras his rank rises further: the Guhyasamāja system places Akṣobhya at the mandala's center, and the primordial Buddha Vajrasattva is identified with him in the Nyingma tradition. His bodhisattva is Vajrapāṇi, the thunderbolt-bearer, and his wrathful faces guard the gates of every tantric mandala. The unshakable monk of the old sūtra became the still point around which the whole esoteric cosmos is arranged.

lore.syncretism: China received him early as Āchù and later rendered him "the Immovable" — a name he shares as a near-doublet with Acala, the blazing Fudō Myōō of Japan, whose wrathful immovability is the mirror image of his serene one. Tibet made Mi bskyod pa central to the highest tantras and to the rites of death and purification, and the five-Buddha system that enthrones him traveled from the Indian universities to every Himalayan valley. Scholars have noted the quiet irony: the least-known of the five in the West is, liturgically, among the most invoked — every vajra-family rite is his household.
lore.culturalLegacy: Akṣobhya's legacy is the mirror itself: the image of mind as a reflecting surface that needs only to stay still became one of the deep metaphors of East Asian Buddhism, from Huayan to Zen. His earth-touching gesture — assigned to him among the five — is the most reproduced Buddha pose on earth, the seal of the historical awakening reassigned to the unshakable one. And his vow remains the tradition's standing definition of patience: not slowness, but a stillness no insult can reach.
lore.extendedMeditation: Akṣobhya is the patron of the unhurried strength: the hand that does not strike back, the mind that registers the insult and lets it pass through like weather through a window frame. He does not ask for indifference — a mirror is not indifferent; it shows everything. He asks for the one thing harder than anger: to see clearly and remain unmoved, and to let clarity, not reaction, do the answering.
lore.archaeology: His oldest document is textual: Lokakṣema's second-century Chinese translation of his sūtra, among the first pure-land scriptures rendered into any language. In stone he belongs to the five-jina program that matured in the eighth and ninth centuries: the eastern niches of Borobudur carry his series in the earth-touching gesture, and the crowns of Nepalese paubhā and Tibetan sculpture place him on the east petal of the jina-mandala. East Javanese bronzes and stone Akṣobhyas — dark, right hand to the earth — are among the finest small Buddhist images in the world.
